🧰 Use AI well · Step 2 of 4 · 5 min

Check before you trust

Why a confident answer can be made up, and three quick checks.

🎭 Fluent is not the same as true

A chatbot's answers are fluent: they are easy to read and sound confident. Inside a chatbot is a language model. It learned from a huge amount of text, and it writes an answer by guessing which word comes next, again and again.

It does not lie on purpose. It simply has no built-in check for truth. So a wrong date, a book that does not exist or a made-up quote can sound just as confident as a true fact.

A confident answer that is made up or wrong is called a hallucination.

A chatbot is often right. That is exactly why its mistakes are easy to miss.

Task. A chatbot gives you a quote, with the author's name and the year. What do these exact details prove?

Show the answer

Right answer: Nothing yet: a model can make up a name, a year and a quote

A name and a year are just what you expect next to a quote, so a model can write them even when the quote is made up. Exact details make an answer look checked, but they prove nothing until you find the quote in a real book or article.

🧪 Three quick checks

A source is where a fact comes from: a book, an article, a website. When a fact from a chatbot matters to you, use three checks:

1. Ask for the source and open it yourself.
2. Find a second source that does not just repeat the first: a textbook, an encyclopedia, an official website.
3. Ask yourself: can this be true? Estimate it with numbers you know.

Another chatbot is not a second source: it guesses words too.

Task. A chatbot says: “A person takes about 100,000 breaths every hour.” Check it. A calm adult takes about 15 breaths a minute. How many breaths is that in one hour?

Show the solution

15 × 60 = 900 breaths in an hour. The chatbot's number is more than a hundred times bigger, so it cannot be right. An estimate with numbers you know catches a mistake like this in seconds.

⚖️ The more harm a mistake can do, the more you check

You do not have to check everything. Ask yourself one question: what happens if this answer is wrong?

A name for a cat: nothing happens, so use it as it is. A fact for a school report: a mistake would spoil your work, so check it.

Health, money, the law, safety: a mistake can do real harm. Never rely on a chatbot alone here. Ask a doctor, another specialist or an adult you trust.

Task. Here are things you might ask a chatbot. What do you do with its answer each time?

Show the solution

A name or a rhyme cannot be false: you only decide whether you like it. A date and a number are facts, so you check them in a source. With medicine and wild mushrooms a mistake can harm you, so the answer must come from a doctor or another person who knows.

🔗 A source can be made up too

Ask for a source, and a chatbot will often name one. But it writes the title of a book or a web address the same way as everything else: by guessing what comes next. So a link may lead to a page that does not exist, or to a page that says something else.

Some chatbots can search the web and show real links. That is better, but your job stays the same: open the page and find the fact there. If it is not there, the fact is still not checked.

If a page looks strange, or asks for a password or for money, close it and tell an adult you trust.

Task. A chatbot gives you a fact and a link to its source. What is the best way to check the fact?

Show the answer

Right answer: Open the link and see whether the page really says this

A chatbot can make up a link, and a real link can lead to a page that says something else. Only the page itself shows what it says. An official-looking address and many details prove nothing, and “Are you sure?” only brings more words from the same chatbot.

Think first. Why not simply ask the chatbot: “Are you sure?”

Show the answer

Because it writes this reply the same way as the first one: by guessing what comes next. How confident it sounds does not tell you whether it is true.

It may find a real mistake. But it may also apologise and change a right answer to a wrong one, or repeat the mistake just as confidently. From inside the chat you cannot tell which happened.

A real check comes from outside the chat: a source you open, a calculation you do, a person who knows.

Task. What is a “hallucination” of an AI model?

Show the answer

Right answer: An answer that sounds confident but is made up or wrong

A language model writes the words that are likely to come next and has no built-in check for truth. So a made-up fact, quote or source can come out in the same confident voice as a true one. The model has no plan to trick you, and nothing is broken.

Task. You need a fact for a school report. Put the steps in a sensible order.

Show the solution
  1. Ask the chatbot for the fact and for its source
  2. Open that source and find the fact there
  3. Find the same fact in a second source
  4. Write it in your own words and name your sources

First the fact and its source, then a look into that source, then a second source. Your own text comes last, so that you write only what you have checked. And when you name your sources, your reader can check you, just as you checked the chatbot.

Remember

  • Fluent is not the same as true. A confident answer that is made up or wrong is called a hallucination.
  • Three checks: ask for the source and open it, find a second source, and ask yourself whether this can be true.
  • The more harm a mistake can do, the more you check. For health, money, the law and safety, ask a specialist or an adult you trust.
  • A real check comes from outside the chat: a source, a calculation, a person who knows.
